title: A Word Of Caution: How Getting Promoted Quietly Turns Off Your Judgment
author: Meller Notes
summary: This piece argues that promotion systematically strips away the informal correction mechanisms that keep judgment sharp early in a career, and that most leaders mistake the resulting silence for alignment. Building on Kahneman's account of judgment biases in Thinking, Fast and Slow, the author's core move is to note what Kahneman left unaddressed: that these biases aren't evenly distributed across a hierarchy, because the social cost of correcting a senior person rises with their seniority even as their objective need for correction stays the same. The piece's central image — a 'mesh of correction' unraveling thread by thread as someone climbs — reframes a boardroom or team going quiet not as evidence of good leadership but as a possible warning sign that dissent has simply become too expensive. It closes by insisting that outside correction for a leader doesn't happen by default; it has to be deliberately engineered against the natural incentive everyone else has to stay quiet.
points: A team that stops pushing back may signal that disagreement has become too costly, not that everyone actually agrees.
Judgment doesn't erode with seniority because the mind gets worse — it erodes because the environment stops supplying correction.
Kahneman's biases are treated as evenly distributed by default, but they concentrate their damage wherever hierarchy suppresses the observer's incentive to speak up.
Because it's structurally easier to see someone else's mistake than your own, a leader's most reliable check is other people — which is exactly what promotion removes.
Rebuilding correction at senior levels has to be deliberate; it will not happen as a byproduct of good intentions.
quotes: A manager corrects the report. A more senior colleague mentions that idea already failed back in 2019. A process catches the bad call before it ever reaches the client.

Then you move up. Promotion after promotion, climbing further into the corporate ladder. And the mesh keeps disappearing, one thread at a time, so slowly that nobody notices the exact moment it happened.
One day you walk out of a hard meeting and realize nobody pushed back on anything. From the top of your ego, that probably reads as a good sign. Alignment. Clarity. The team gets it.
Daniel Kahneman spent 500 pages mapping the systematic errors of human judgment in Thinking, Fast and Slow. We covered them last week.
It's far easier to spot someone else's mistake than your own. The observer isn't under pressure, has nothing riding on the outcome, doesn't need the story to sound good.
Not because your mind gets worse. Because the environment stops correcting you.
In a leadership seat, it doesn't happen on its own. It has to be built on purpose, against the incentive of nearly everyone around you.
